content:
When you hire church staff, your church takes on employer responsibilities. Federal income-tax exemption does not remove the need to handle employment taxes correctly.

Start by separating ordinary employee payroll from clergy tax treatment. IRS Publication 517 explains why a minister can be an employee for income-tax purposes while paying self-employment tax on ministerial earnings.

---

## Identify the employer and payroll owner

Before hiring employees, confirm that your church has an Employer Identification Number, or EIN. Use the church's EIN on employment-tax filings and payments, rather than a staff member's Social Security number.

Assign someone to monitor payroll tax payments and IRS correspondence even if you hire a payroll service. The IRS holds the employer responsible when a payroll service fails to deposit its taxes. Keep the church's address on its IRS account so tax notices reach you directly.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"The laborer is worthy of his wages."* — 1 Timothy 5:18 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Classify the work before entering payroll

Under the IRS common-law rule, a worker is generally your employee when you have the right to control what they do and how they do it. Giving someone freedom in daily work does not remove that right of control.

Review the actual working relationship before choosing employee or contractor reporting. Publication 15 directs employers to the worker-classification guidance in Publication 15-A. For wages paid to employees, use Form W-2 rather than a Form 1099.

Part-time employees and employees hired for short periods receive the same federal employment-tax treatment as full-time employees. Review a part-time administrator's status using the work arrangement, rather than assuming a small schedule makes the person a contractor.

---

## Set clergy tax treatment separately

Ask your CPA or payroll provider to review the minister's credentials and duties against Publication 517. Its definition includes duly ordained, commissioned or licensed ministers and describes the religious functions they must be authorized to perform.

| Situation | Federal treatment to review |
|---|---|
| Minister employed by the congregation and paid a salary | Generally an employee with wages for income-tax purposes |
| Earnings for ministerial services | Generally subject to self-employment tax under SECA, rather than FICA, unless an applicable exception applies |
| Church employee outside the clergy categories in Publication 517 | Wages generally subject to Social Security and Medicare under FICA, subject to exceptions |

A qualifying minister's salary for ministerial services is not subject to mandatory federal income-tax withholding. A minister who is a common-law employee may agree with the church to voluntary withholding to cover income and self-employment taxes. Otherwise, estimated tax payments may be needed. Have the minister and tax adviser settle that arrangement before setting withholding.

<Callout type="warning">
Use a payroll provider or CPA familiar with Publication 517 to review clergy settings. Self-employment tax treatment of ministerial earnings does not, by itself, make the minister an independent contractor for income-tax purposes. Review any claimed exemption against the IRS requirements before changing coverage.
</Callout>

---

## Document a housing allowance before payment

If you include a ministerial housing allowance, the employing church must officially designate a definite amount before paying it. The church cannot decide the amount after the payment. Keep the designation in an employment contract, church minutes, budget or another official action taken before payment.

Designation alone does not make the entire allowance excludable. For a minister who owns a home, Publication 517 limits the income-tax exclusion to the smallest of the amount actually used to provide a home, the officially designated amount, or the home's fair rental value including furnishings and utilities. The allowance must also stay within reasonable compensation for the services.

The housing exclusion applies to income tax, not self-employment tax. Have the CPA check eligibility and the exclusion calculation rather than marking every housing payment tax-free.

---

## Complete the hiring paperwork

Use this checklist when you bring an employee onto payroll:

- [ ] Record the employee's name and Social Security number correctly for wage reporting.
- [ ] For employees subject to federal income-tax withholding, obtain a signed Form W-4 when work starts and apply it to the first wage payment.
- [ ] Have the employee complete and sign Section 1 of Form I-9 no later than the first day of employment.
- [ ] Complete Section 2 within three business days after that first day. For employment lasting less than three business days, complete it no later than the first day.
- [ ] Provide the I-9 instructions and Lists of Acceptable Documents. Let the employee choose which acceptable documentation to present.

Keep the completed I-9; do not mail it to USCIS. Follow its instructions for document examination and any applicable reverification.

---

## Check state requirements independently

Ask your state revenue and labor agencies which employer registrations, withholding rules and employment programs apply to your church. Include the employee's work location and residence in that inquiry. Do not assume the federal payroll settings answer the state questions.

New Jersey illustrates the separate steps. Its registration guidance includes Form NJ-REG for tax and employer registration. Its withholding guidance addresses resident employees and nonresidents working in the state, with exceptions. New Jersey Child Support also requires reports of newly hired and rehired employees to the state directory. Use your own state's agency instructions for the reporting method and deadline.

Federal unemployment tax is another distinct question. Organizations exempt under section 501(c)(3) are exempt from FUTA. Check state unemployment obligations separately with the state agency.

---

## Prepare each pay run and filing calendar

For staff subject to ordinary withholding, use Form W-4 and the IRS withholding methods to calculate federal income tax. Account for the employee and employer portions of Social Security and Medicare where applicable. Apply the separately reviewed clergy treatment to ministerial earnings.

Determine the church's federal deposit schedule under Publication 15. Deposit timing follows tax-liability rules, not how often you pay staff. Federal tax deposits must be electronic; filing a return is a separate responsibility.

Generally, report federal income-tax withholding and FICA on quarterly Form 941. Use annual Form 944 only after receiving the IRS's written notice authorizing that filing. Plan for wage statements and SSA reporting too.

<Callout type="important">
Tax guidance checked October 15, 2026. The IRS's general deadline to file 2026 Forms W-2 and W-3 with the SSA and furnish employee W-2 copies is February 1, 2027. Confirm the current deadline, withholding figures and deposit rules with the IRS, and state requirements with the relevant state agencies, before processing payroll.
</Callout>

---

## Keep records and verify the service's work

Retain employment-tax records for at least four years. Publication 15 calls for wage amounts and dates, employee information, withholding certificates, tax-deposit details and copies of returns with confirmation numbers. Keep records of fringe benefits and expense reimbursements, including substantiation.

Reconcile annual wage reporting with the employment-tax returns using the IRS instructions. The reconciliation compares income tax withheld, Social Security and Medicare wages, and those taxes; employer and employee tax portions need different treatment in that comparison.

<Callout type="tip">
Ask your payroll service how you can verify federal deposits yourself through EFTPS. The IRS recommends that employers retain their own access and periodically check payments. Follow up immediately on a missed or late deposit rather than waiting for year-end forms.
</Callout>
excerpt: Set up staff payroll with clear clergy tax treatment, hiring forms, state checks, deposit oversight and employment-tax records.
title: Setting Up Payroll for Church Staff

sources.claim: Opening and section 1: tax-exempt employers need an EIN and have employment-tax responsibilities.
sources.quote: Before an organization becomes an employer and hires employees, it needs a federal Employer Identification Number (EIN)

sources.claim: Opening and sections 6–7: tax exemption does not remove employment-tax obligations; federal, state and local taxes must be considered.
sources.quote: If the organization has employees, it is responsible for several federal, state, and local taxes.

sources.claim: Section 1: use the employer EIN rather than an SSN on tax returns and payments.
sources.quote: Use your EIN on all of the items you send to the IRS and the SSA.

sources.claim: Section 1: do not substitute a personal SSN for the employer EIN.
sources.quote: Don’t use an SSN in place of an EIN.

sources.claim: Section 1: assign oversight even with an ordinary payroll service; employer remains responsible for deposits.
sources.quote: The employer is ultimately responsible for the deposit and payment of federal tax liabilities.

sources.claim: Section 1: keep church address for IRS notices.
sources.quote: The IRS strongly suggests that the employer does not change their address of record to that of the payroll service provider as it may significantly limit the employer's ability to be informed of tax matters involving their business.

sources.claim: Scripture callout: exact excerpt of 1 Timothy 5:18, verified in the official single-verse reader.
sources.publisher: The Lockman Foundation, Legacy Standard Bible
sources.quote: The laborer is worthy of his wages.

sources.claim: Section 2: common-law control of what and how, even with worker freedom.
sources.quote: Generally, a worker who performs services for you is your employee if you have the right to control what will be done and how it will be done. This is so even when you give the employee freedom of action.

sources.claim: Section 2: review the relationship with the guidance IRS identifies.
sources.quote: See Pub. 15-A for more information on how to determine whether an individual providing services is an independent contractor or an employee.

sources.claim: Section 2: employee wage reporting uses W-2, not 1099.
sources.quote: Generally, don’t use Forms 1099 to report wages and other compensation you paid to employees; report these on Form W-2.

sources.claim: Section 2: part-time and short-term work alone do not change federal employment-tax treatment.
sources.quote: Part-time workers and workers hired for short periods of time are treated the same as full-time employees for federal income tax withholding and social security, Medicare, and FUTA tax purposes.

sources.claim: Section 3: review credentials and religious functions for minister definition; basis for professional setup review.
sources.quote: Ministers are individuals who are duly ordained, commissioned, or licensed by a religious body constituting a church or church denomination. Ministers have the authority to conduct religious worship, perform sacerdotal functions, and administer ordinances or sacraments according to the prescribed tenets and practices of that church or denomination.

sources.claim: Opening, section 3 table and warning: salaried congregational minister generally employee for income tax; SECA is not contractor classification.
sources.quote: If a congregation employs you and pays you a salary, you are generally a common-law employee and income from the exercise of your ministry is wages for income tax purposes.

sources.claim: Section 3 table and sections 7 setup: ministerial earnings under SECA, not FICA, subject to applicable exceptions.
sources.quote: The services you perform in the exercise of your ministry, of the duties required by your religious order, or of your profession as a Christian Science practitioner or reader are covered by social security and Medicare under SECA.

sources.claim: Section 3: ministerial earnings are exempt from FICA and covered by SECA absent exemption; quote from Table 1 minister row.
sources.quote: NO. Your ministerial earnings are exempt.

sources.claim: Section 3: exceptions exist, and exemptions require IRS approval; professional should review rather than assume coverage.
sources.quote: You ask the IRS for an exemption from SE tax for your services and the IRS approves your request.

sources.claim: Section 3 table: nonclergy church employees generally subject to FICA with exceptions.
sources.quote: If you are a religious worker (a church employee) and aren't in one of the classes already discussed, your wages are generally subject to social security and Medicare tax under FICA, not SECA. Some exceptions are discussed next.

sources.claim: Section 3: qualifying ministerial salary is outside mandatory federal income-tax withholding, subject to the two conditions quoted.
sources.quote: However, your salary isn't subject to federal income tax withholding if both of the following conditions apply. You are a duly ordained, commissioned, or licensed minister, a member of a religious order (who hasn't taken a vow of poverty), or a Christian Science practitioner or reader. Your salary is for ministerial services

sources.claim: Section 3: common-law employee ministers may use voluntary withholding covering income and SE tax.
sources.quote: If you perform your services as a common-law employee of the church and your salary isn't subject to income tax withholding, you can enter into a voluntary withholding agreement with the church to cover any income and SE tax that may be due.

sources.claim: Section 3: estimated tax may be needed without adequate withholding; settle arrangement with adviser.
sources.quote: If your salary isn't subject to withholding, or if you don't pay enough tax through withholding, you may need to make estimated tax payments to avoid penalties for not paying enough tax as you earn your income.

sources.claim: Section 4: definite official housing designation precedes payment, cannot be retroactive.
sources.quote: The church or organization that employs you must officially designate the payment as a housing allowance before it makes the payment. It must designate a definite amount. It can't determine the amount of the housing allowance at a later date.

sources.claim: Section 4: official designation documentation options.
sources.quote: An official designation of an amount as a housing or rental allowance may be shown in an employment contract, in the minutes of a church or qualified organization, in a budget, or in any official action taken in advance of payment of the allowance.

sources.claim: Section 4: homeowner housing exclusion is limited to smallest listed amount.
sources.quote: If you own your home and you receive as part of your salary a housing or rental allowance, you may exclude from gross income the smallest of: The amount actually used to provide a home; The amount officially designated as a rental allowance; or The fair rental value of the home, including furnishings, utilities, garage, etc.

sources.claim: Section 4: housing allowance cannot exceed reasonable pay.
sources.quote: The amount isn't more than reasonable pay for your services.

sources.claim: Section 4: housing exclusion affects income tax only, not SE tax.
sources.quote: This exclusion applies only for income tax purposes. It doesn't apply for SE tax purposes

sources.claim: Section 5: correct name and Social Security number for wage reporting.
sources.quote: You’re required to get each employee’s name and SSN and to enter them on Form W-2.

sources.claim: Sections 5 and 7: signed W-4 when staff start; first payment effective.
sources.quote: Ask all new employees to give you a signed Form W-4 when they start work. Make the form effective with the first wage payment.

sources.claim: Section 5: first-day deadline for Section 1.
sources.quote: Employees must complete and sign Section 1 of Form I-9 no later than the first day of employment

sources.claim: Section 5: Section 2 deadline and short-employment exception.
sources.quote: Complete Section 2 within three business days after the employee's first day of employment. If you hire an individual for less than three business days, complete Section 2 no later than the first day of employment.

sources.claim: Section 5: make I-9 instructions and document list available, including reverification.
sources.quote: Make the instructions for Form I-9 and Lists of Acceptable Documents available to the employee when completing the Form I-9 and when requesting that the employee present documentation to complete Supplement B, Reverification and Rehire.

sources.claim: Section 5: employee chooses acceptable I-9 documentation.
sources.quote: An employer cannot specify which documentation you may present from the Lists of Acceptable Documents.

sources.claim: Section 5: retain I-9, do not mail to USCIS; follow applicable reverification.
sources.quote: Retain completed forms.

sources.claim: Section 5: retain rather than mail completed forms.
sources.quote: Do not mail completed forms to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

sources.claim: Section 5: review examination and reverification requirements.
sources.quote: Complete Supplement B, Reverification and Rehire when applicable.

sources.claim: Section 6: labeled New Jersey example, employer tax registration is separate.
sources.publisher: New Jersey Division of Revenue and Enterprise Services
sources.quote: Second, after filing the certificate of formation/authorization, file the tax/employer registration form (Form NJ-REG).

sources.claim: Section 6: work location and residence matter in NJ; state withholding exceptions.
sources.quote: All New Jersey resident employees, unless they're already being taxed in another state at a higher rate.

sources.claim: Section 6: nonresident work in NJ and exceptions, demonstrating why to ask your own state agencies.
sources.quote: Nonresident employees working in New Jersey, or those who telework here for their convenience . Pennsylvania residents working in New Jersey are an exception, but they need to fill out a form Employee's Certificate of Nonresidence in New Jersey to qualify.

sources.claim: Section 6: NJ new and rehired workers reported to state directory; no nationwide deadline asserted.
sources.quote: Federal and state law requires employers to report newly hired and rehired employees to the New Jersey State Directory of New Hire (NJSDNH) within 20 days of hire.

sources.claim: Section 6: FUTA exemption for section 501(c)(3) organizations.
sources.quote: An organization that is exempt from income tax under section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code is also exempt from FUTA.

sources.claim: Section 7: W-4 and IRS methods determine ordinary employee income-tax withholding.
sources.quote: An organization generally must withhold federal income tax from its employees’ wages. To figure how much to withhold from each wage payment, the organization should use the employee's Form W-4 PDF and the methods described in Publication 15, (Circular E), Employer’s Tax Guide PDF and Publication 15-A, Employer’s Supplemental Tax Guide PDF

sources.claim: Section 7: ordinary employee FICA share and employer matching obligations.
sources.quote: The organization, as the employer, must withhold and deposit the employee’s part of the taxes and pay a matching amount.

sources.claim: Section 7: deposit schedule is separate from pay frequency; establish calendar.
sources.quote: Your deposit schedule isn’t determined by how often you pay your employees or make deposits.

sources.claim: Section 7: electronic federal deposits.
sources.quote: You must use EFT to make all federal tax deposits.

sources.claim: Section 7: tax reporting on quarterly Form 941, separately from deposits.
sources.quote: Report federal income taxes, Social Security, and Medicare taxes on Form 941, Employer’s Quarterly Federal Tax

sources.claim: Section 7: Form 944 only after written IRS notice.
sources.quote: You must receive written notice from the IRS to file Form 944 instead of quarterly Forms 941 before you may file this form.

sources.claim: Section 7 volatile callout: exact 2026 SSA filing deadline, as of 2026-10-15.
sources.quote: The due date for filing 2026 Forms W-2, W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU, W-2VI, W-3, and W-3SS with the SSA is February 1, 2027, whether you file using paper forms or electronically.

sources.claim: Section 7 volatile callout: general employee W-2 furnishing deadline for 2026 statements.
sources.quote: Generally, you must furnish Copies B, C, and 2 of Form W-2 to your employees by February 1, 2027.

sources.claim: Section 8: general federal employment-tax record retention minimum.
sources.quote: Keep all records of employment taxes for at least 4 years.

sources.claim: Section 8: wage and worker information records.
sources.quote: Amounts and dates of all wage, annuity, and pension payments.

sources.claim: Section 8: employee information records.
sources.quote: Names, addresses, SSNs, and occupations of employees and recipients.

sources.claim: Section 8: copies of withholding certificates.
sources.quote: Copies of employees’ and recipients’ federal income tax withholding certificates (Forms W-4, W-4P, W-4R, W-4S, and W-4V).

sources.claim: Section 8: deposit, filing and reimbursement evidence.
sources.quote: Dates and amounts of tax deposits you made and acknowledgment numbers for deposits made by EFTPS. Copies of returns filed and confirmation numbers. Records of fringe benefits and expense reimbursements provided to your employees, including substantiation.

sources.claim: Section 8: compare W-3 and 941/944 by income tax and FICA wages/taxes; distinguish employer and employee portions.
sources.quote: Reconcile Form W-3 with your four quarterly Forms 941, annual Form 943, or annual Form 944 by comparing amounts reported for the following items. Federal income tax withheld. Social security and Medicare wages. Social security and Medicare taxes.

sources.claim: Section 8: reconciliation is not simply equality of every tax amount.
sources.quote: Forms 941, Form 943, and Form 944 report both the employer and employee social security and Medicare taxes while Form W-3 reports only the employee taxes.

sources.claim: Section 8 tip: employers retain EFTPS access and check service deposits independently.
sources.quote: Employers should register on the EFTPS system to get their own PIN and use this PIN to periodically verify payments.

sources.claim: Section 8 tip: follow up on late or missed payment immediately.
sources.quote: A red flag should go up the first time a service provider misses a payment or makes a late payment.

claim_check.notes: Author source mapping and exact-quote checks complete; independent Opus review of claims, scripture and desktop/mobile previews is required. Federal and New Jersey guidance checked 2026-10-15; Publication 15 is 2026, Publication 517 is 2025, and W-2/W-3 instructions cover tax year 2026.

rulings: US federal payroll-tax setup only; New Jersey is a labeled example. Readers must confirm their own state rules. Avoid treating one state's rules as national requirements.

No provider rankings, tax rates, wage bases or individual estimated-tax calculations; refer clergy eligibility, exceptions and housing calculations to a CPA or payroll provider. Keep the article to verified employer setup, without personalized tax advice or methodology rulings.
